verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Thrissur ayurvedic units with tight monthly stock-and-receivable control; avoid small proprietary-brand units with no herb-supply visibility.
title: Thrissur ayurvedic & herbal products: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**Ayurvedic and herbal units turn herbs, oils and packaging into tablets, syrups, oils and pastes, and cash comes back slowly.** A peer rating describes a manufacturer running over 1500 products across these formats [9]. The same rating house flags the core cash problem: long credit to customers, partly offset by supplier credit, with inventory at 142 days in FY2023 against 77 days in FY2022 after raw-material stocking [10]. So when a proposal lands, check the receivable days and the herb-stocking logic separately; if inventory has jumped without a matching order book, ask why the stocking was done.

## What has changed now
**The national demand picture is weak while credit is still expanding fast, so the risk is a slow-moving stock book financed by debt.** India-wide output is -2.1% Apr-to-date while bank credit is +21.6% YoY, a gap of +23.7 pp [D]. Kerala is the better half: GST collections +10.3% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D]. **Thrissur-specific data is thin — the local sources are an Oushadhi 85th-anniversary event [2] and a coriander-leaf mandi page [3], neither of which tells us about ayurvedic demand.** Lean on first principles and peers here.

## Where the growth is
**Peer results show the growth is in contract manufacturing and export-led herbal cosmetics, not in undifferentiated domestic brands.** Accretion Nutraveda reports revenue up 109.35% YoY and EBITDA up 88.03% for H1 FY27 [4][5]; Veerhealth Care reports 388% YoY revenue growth in Q1 FY27 on export sales and new categories [7]. Pursue Thrissur units that manufacture for other brands, hold repeat institutional orders, or export herbal cosmetics. Avoid small proprietary-brand units selling only into local retail with no order visibility.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the working-capital cycle, because that is where this industry loses money.** Take monthly stock statements and ageing of receivables, and a quarterly herb-purchase register reconciled to sales. Price the limit off the 142-day inventory reality [10], not the borrower's optimistic cycle. Where the borrower exports, take the shipping bill and remittance trail each month. Collect from customer the actual receivable days, herb-supplier credit terms and any regulatory licence status — the rating note flags regulatory exposure as a live risk [10].

## Early-warning signs
**Watch inventory days and receivable ageing first; they move before default.** If inventory days cross the borrower's own prior-year figure without new orders, cut the limit and ask for the order book. If a large customer's payment slips one cycle, move to cash-on-delivery terms for new dispatches. If herb prices spike, check whether the borrower can pass it on — the rating methodology notes raw material is the largest cost component for such companies [11].
watch: Inventory days rise above prior year with no new orders -> freeze fresh limits and seek order book
Any single customer slips one full cycle -> shift new dispatches to cash or LC
GST turnover falls below bank credit growth for two months -> ask for revised projections and reduce limit
Purchase register shows stocking without matching sales -> require sell-through evidence before renewal
Shipping bills without matching remittances -> stop export packing credit
